Crabb sponsored Ordinance 25-040, which the Council adopted on 12 August 2025 by nine votes to one. It makes it unlawful to camp on any public property in Columbus, and it defines camping to include sleeping, or preparing to sleep, anywhere from a street or park to the space under a bridge. Someone who breaks it is punished on conviction in the recorder’s court, so the penalty is a criminal one rather than a fine. She also moved the amendment that requires police to give written or oral notice and eight days to leave before anyone is removed. One qualification a reader should weigh: that notice period is a real softening of how the ban is enforced, and it was her own amendment, so she backed both the prohibition and the warning that goes with it.

The camping ordinance Crabb sponsored sets what is prohibited and how it is enforced. It commits no money, and this question asks how much a community should spend on housing and services. She questioned United Way on how camps are closed and what services are offered, but asked for no funding level of her own.

It does not choose between the two that remain — subsidies and tax breaks to get affordable housing built, or leaving supply and price to the market. Seating either would assert something she has not said.

On 24 October 2023 Crabb told the Council that, as a realtor and property manager, she could assure them rent control would not benefit affordable housing but would do the opposite. Two weeks earlier the Council had taken up Resolution 373-23, which asked Georgia’s legislature to let cities and counties adopt local anti-displacement rules in economically depressed areas. She moved it, then voted No on it before the final count was taken, and the Council rescinded the resolution altogether at the later meeting. Her objection is to rent control as such, not to its scope: she does not argue for keeping it on subsidised housing only, and her vote was against Columbus even asking for the power.

In October 2025 Crabb was one of the councillors who voted to ask Georgia's legislature to pass House Bill 601, the Georgia Gun Safe Act. The Council adopted Resolution 340-25 with nobody against. The bill would stop licensed dealers, manufacturers, importers and gun show vendors from selling or transferring assault weapons anywhere in Georgia from July 2025 until January 2036, and it defines an assault weapon to include a semi-automatic rifle under thirty inches long and a semi-automatic centre-fire rifle that takes a detachable magazine and has a feature such as a protruding grip, a thumbhole or folding stock, or a threaded barrel. Other firearms stay lawful to buy and to own, which is what separates this position from a broader ban. The same bill would also set up a state firearms registry, raise the purchase age and require carry licences to be renewed each year. Two things a reader should weigh: a Columbus councillor cannot regulate firearms, because Georgia law reserves that to the state, so this is the Council stating a view rather than using a power of its own; and the ban it endorses is on sales by dealers rather than on owning a weapon already held.
